slots.label: truth-probability misconception
slots.description: 80% power means there is an 80% chance the hypothesis or significant result is true.
slots.repair: Power assumes a specified effect is true and asks how often the test detects it; it does not tell whether the effect is true.
slots.repairQuestion: In a power calculation, is the specified effect assumed or concluded?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says the effect is assumed for the calculation, not proven or assigned 80% truth probability.

slots.label: effect-free power
slots.description: A study simply has 80% power in general, without specifying an effect size or test.
slots.repair: Power is always for a specified effect size, alpha, sample size, variability, and analysis plan.
slots.repairQuestion: What information is missing if someone only says 'this study has 80% power'?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner names the needed effect size and design/test conditions.

slots.label: post-hoc-excuse misconception
slots.description: After a nonsignificant result, observed post-hoc power proves there was no effect or proves the study failed only because of low power.
slots.repair: Power is most useful before data collection for a meaningful effect size. A nonsignificant result must be interpreted with design, interval estimates, assumptions, and uncertainty.
slots.repairQuestion: Why is power analysis usually more informative before the study than after seeing the result?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says power is a planning tool tied to assumed effects and observed results need confidence intervals or uncertainty, not just post-hoc power.

Power is a design property: the probability of detecting a specified true effect with a specified test and alpha. It depends on sample size, effect size, variability, alpha, and design. It is not the probability that a hypothesis or result is true, and it must be tied to a meaningful effect size.
